opus-5.5.text:
I think our biggest strength is that we sit right at the intersection of systems and machine learning, and we take both sides seriously. A lot of teams are strong in one direction: either they're very good at model research, or they're very good at infrastructure engineering. What we try to do is co-design. When we think about inference, for example, we don't just treat the model as a black box and optimize kernels underneath it. We look at how people actually use these models, things like multi-turn conversations, agents, structured outputs, and long contexts, and then design the runtime and scheduling around those patterns. A lot of our performance gains come from that full-stack view rather than from one clever trick.

The second strength is the open-source community. From the beginning we've built in the open, so we get very fast feedback. People deploy our work in production at real scale, they hit problems we would never see in a lab, and they report them or even contribute fixes. That loop makes us move much faster than a closed team of similar size. It also keeps us honest, because if something is slow or buggy, people tell you immediately.

Third, I'd say it's the people and the culture. The team is fairly small, very hands-on, and has a strong academic background, but everyone is also willing to do the unglamorous engineering work. We care about rigor: benchmarking carefully, comparing fairly, not over-claiming. At the same time, we ship quickly. Being both research-minded and execution-minded is rarer than you might think.

Of course, there are areas where bigger companies have advantages, like massive compute resources and large dedicated teams. We can't compete on sheer scale, so we compete on speed, focus, and community. In this field things change every few months, so being able to adapt quickly is often more valuable than being the largest.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts teams focused on model research or infrastructure, but does not acknowledge that other teams could claim the same positive qualities.

r002.rationale: It describes Ying Sheng’s team culture, but does not say that each team develops its own distinctive culture.

fable-5.1.text:
I think our biggest strength is that we started from the actual problem rather than from a research agenda. SGLang came out of us sitting with real workloads, agent loops, multi-turn chat, structured output, and noticing how much redundant computation everyone was doing. Things like RadixAttention for prefix caching weren't clever for the sake of being clever; they fell out of looking at traces and asking why the same prefix was being recomputed thousands of times.

The second thing is that the core team is small and very hands-on with systems. A lot of us have spent years inside the kernel and scheduler layer, so when we talk about a feature we can usually go from idea to a working implementation in days, and then we're measuring it on real hardware, not just in a paper. That tight loop matters a lot in inference right now, because the hardware and the models are both moving every few months.

And then honestly, the community. We're open source, and a lot of the best contributions, quantization support, new model architectures, speculative decoding improvements, have come from people outside the original group, including folks at companies deploying it in production. That gives us a feedback signal that's hard to get any other way. Other teams have more people or more money, and I respect what they've built. But I'd say our edge is that we're close to the metal and close to the users at the same time, and we try hard to keep the codebase simple enough that someone can read it in a weekend and start contributing.

astra-6.text: I think our strength is how closely we connect research with engineering. We’re interested in new ideas, but we also ask what it takes to make those ideas work in practice. That means testing assumptions early, understanding the bottlenecks, and letting what we learn from implementation guide the next research question. Other teams have their own strengths; for us, that close feedback loop is especially valuable.

sol-6.1.text: I think our strength is how closely we connect research with engineering. It’s one thing to have a promising idea, and another to make it work reliably under real constraints. We try to keep that feedback loop short: test an idea, understand where it breaks, and use that to guide the next step. Other teams have their own strengths, so I wouldn’t say we’re better across the board. For us, the advantage is being able to learn and iterate together.
